topics.title: Question Approach and Source Analysis
topics.notesHtml:
General Approach to Source-Based Questions

  • Look out for symbols and messages in the source.
  • Look out for source provenance (when the source was created and who created it).
  • Identify the characters and what is going on in the source.
  • Identify possible hidden messages.
  • Your analysis of the source must always be accurate and clear. Be discerning to interpret the source accurately and quickly.
  • Always look out for the question issue/main issue in the source (above background information) and address it - this is your inference point, what you need to infer about.

Example: "What can you learn from this source about the Korean War?" - the focus must be on the Korean War itself, not on China's role or America's actions specifically.

  • Require sufficient facts (1-2 lines) to support your inference.

flashcards.q: What two things about the source's provenance should you look out for first?
flashcards.a: When the source was created and who created it.

flashcards.q: Besides provenance, what four things should you look out for in a source?
flashcards.a: Symbols and messages, characters and what is going on, possible hidden messages, and the question issue/main issue.

flashcards.q: Where should you look for the question issue/main issue?
flashcards.a: Above the background information, in the source itself - this is your inference point, what you need to infer about.

flashcards.q: How many lines of facts are typically needed to support an inference?
flashcards.a: 1-2 lines of sufficient facts.

flashcards.q: If a question asks 'What can you learn from this source about the Korean War?', what should the focus be?
flashcards.a: The Korean War itself, not on a specific country's role or actions (e.g. not just China's role or America's actions).

flashcards.q: What quality must your analysis of a source always have?
flashcards.a: It must always be accurate and clear.

flashcards.q: What skill is needed to interpret a source accurately?
flashcards.a: Being discerning, so you can interpret the source accurately and quickly.

flashcards.q: What are the two main things a source's provenance reveals?
flashcards.a: The time the source was created and the identity of its creator.

quiz.question: When approaching a source-based question, what should you identify first alongside symbols and messages?
choices: Source provenance (when and by whom created)
quiz.explanation: The notes state to look out for symbols/messages and source provenance (when created and who created it).

quiz.question: For the question 'What can you learn from this source about the Korean War?', where should the focus be?
quiz.explanation: The notes give this exact example, clarifying the focus must be on the Korean War itself, not a specific country's role.

quiz.question: Where is the 'question issue' or main issue typically found?
choices: Above the background information, within the source
quiz.explanation: The notes say to always look for the question issue/main issue in the source, above background information - this is the inference point.

quiz.question: How much factual support is generally required for an inference?
quiz.explanation: The notes specify requiring sufficient facts (1-2 lines) to support your inference.

quiz.question: What quality must your source analysis always maintain?
quiz.explanation: The notes state your analysis must always be accurate and clear.

shortAnswer.prompt: Explain the general approach you should take before answering any source-based question.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Before answering, examine the source for symbols and messages, note its provenance (when it was created and by whom), identify the characters and what is happening, and look for any hidden messages. Then locate the question issue or main issue within the source itself, above the background information, as this is the actual inference point you must address. Ensure your analysis is accurate, clear, and supported by 1-2 lines of sufficient facts.
rubric: Mentions checking symbols/messages and provenance (when/who created)
Mentions identifying characters and hidden messages
Mentions locating the question issue/main issue as the inference point
Mentions the need for accurate, clear analysis with 1-2 lines of factual support

topics.title: Inference
topics.notesHtml:
Types of Questions

  • What is the message?
  • What is the cartoonist trying to convey?

Other Possible Questions

  • Sentiments (feelings - e.g. proud, patriotic, pity, disgusted, etc.)
  • Attitudes (similar to tone - e.g. critical, harsh, pessimistic, condemnatory, etc.)
  • Tone (e.g. sceptical, cynical, optimistic, pessimistic, melancholic, frustrated, anger, disapproving - note that 'positive' and 'negative' are not considered tone)

Structure

Single paragraph with context, or 2 paragraphs with context included. The number of paragraphs depends on the richness of the source.

  1. Message (Infer)
  2. Evidence (provide a quotation or description of the source)
  3. Explanation (elaborate the link between your quotation and inference)
  4. Link (can be before or after context)
  5. Context (support with contextual knowledge, which must be in sync and relevant/aligned with your inference)

Example starting sentence: "The message of the source..."

Notes

  • [6 Marks] (spend about 10-12 minutes on this question, but no more)
  • Also known as 'Message' questions.
  • Always look for the bigger picture of the entire written or picture source. Don't point out only one small aspect of the source.
  • Do not make one-word inferences.
  • Ensure you do not repeat any of the words found in the source in your inference (do not describe the source).
  • Repeat keywords found in the question (always answer or link back to the question).
  • When the source is a picture or cartoon, always infer first and then describe the source. If there are speech bubbles, or accompanying text like a caption, you must quote them in your answer.
  • Always think about a factor or perspective that you have learnt and try to make an inference that relates to it (avoid absurd or overly simple inferences).

flashcards.q: How many marks are Inference questions typically worth?
flashcards.a: 6 marks.

flashcards.q: How much time should be spent on an Inference question?
flashcards.a: About 10-12 minutes, but no more.

flashcards.q: What is another name for Inference questions?
flashcards.a: 'Message' questions.

flashcards.q: What are the four components of the Inference structure?
flashcards.a: Message (Infer), Evidence (quotation/description), Explanation (link quotation to inference), Link/Context (contextual knowledge support).

flashcards.q: What is a good starting sentence for an Inference answer?
flashcards.a: "The message of the source..."

flashcards.q: What other types of questions fall under Inference besides 'What is the message?'
flashcards.a: Sentiments, attitudes, and tone questions.

flashcards.q: Name two examples of 'tone' words mentioned in the notes.
flashcards.a: Sceptical, cynical, optimistic, pessimistic, melancholic, frustrated, anger, disapproving (any two).

flashcards.q: Why are 'positive' and 'negative' not acceptable as tone descriptions?
flashcards.a: Because they are not considered tone according to the notes.

flashcards.q: What mistake should you avoid regarding the size of your inference (the 'bigger picture')?
flashcards.a: Don't point out only one small aspect of the source - always look for the bigger picture of the entire source.

flashcards.q: What should you avoid repeating in your inference answer?
flashcards.a: Any of the words found in the source (do not describe the source).

flashcards.q: What should you do with keywords found in the question?
flashcards.a: Repeat them - always answer or link back to the question.

flashcards.q: When the source is a picture or cartoon, what order should you follow?
flashcards.a: Always infer first and then describe the source.

flashcards.q: What must you do if there are speech bubbles or captions in a picture source?
flashcards.a: You must quote them in your answer.

flashcards.q: What should you try to connect your inference to, to avoid absurd inferences?
flashcards.a: A factor or perspective that you have learnt.

quiz.explanation: The notes state Inference questions are worth 6 marks.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as an acceptable tone descriptor in the notes?
quiz.explanation: The notes explicitly state that 'positive' and 'negative' are not considered tone.

quiz.question: When the source is a cartoon with speech bubbles, what must you do?
quiz.explanation: The notes state if there are speech bubbles or accompanying text, you must quote them in your answer.

quiz.question: What is the correct order when analysing a picture or cartoon source for inference?
choices: Infer first, then describe the source
quiz.explanation: The notes state that when the source is a picture or cartoon, always infer first and then describe the source.

quiz.question: What is a common mistake to avoid when making inferences?
choices: Repeating words found in the source itself
quiz.explanation: The notes warn against repeating any of the words found in the source in your inference, as this becomes mere description.

quiz.question: What is another name for the Inference question type?
quiz.explanation: The notes state Inference questions are also known as 'Message' questions.

shortAnswer.prompt: Describe the structure you should use to answer an Inference/Message question, and explain one key pitfall to avoid.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: An Inference answer should be written in a single paragraph (or two if the source is rich), following the sequence: Message (state your inference), Evidence (quote or describe the relevant part of the source), Explanation (elaborate the link between the evidence and your inference), and Link/Context (support with relevant contextual knowledge that aligns with your inference). One key pitfall to avoid is repeating words found in the source in your inference statement, as this becomes description rather than inference; instead, use your own words and repeat keywords from the question to stay focused on answering it directly.
rubric: States the message-evidence-explanation-context structure
Notes the paragraph should address the bigger picture, not one small aspect
Identifies the pitfall of repeating source words instead of inferring
Mentions repeating question keywords to answer directly

shortAnswer.prompt: Why should you always try to link your inference to a factor or perspective you have learnt?
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Linking the inference to a factor or perspective you have studied ensures the inference is grounded in meaningful historical understanding rather than being an absurd or overly simple one-word observation. It helps demonstrate deeper contextual understanding and produces a more substantial, well-supported message rather than merely describing the source.
rubric: Explains that this avoids absurd or overly simple inferences
Connects to demonstrating contextual/historical understanding
References the notes' caution against one-word inferences

topics.title: Inference with Purpose
topics.notesHtml:
Types of Questions

  • Why was this cartoon published?
  • What is the intention of the cartoonist in publishing this source?
  • Is the cartoonist an opponent or supporter of the issue?

Structure

One paragraph will suffice if well written and elaborated upon.

Example starting sentence: "The source was published to influence/educate/persuade/criticise/justify..."

Notes

  • [7 Marks] (spend about 10-12 minutes on this question, but no more)
  • Also known as 'Why' questions.
  • Do not make one-word inferences.
  • Ensure you do not repeat any of the words found in the source in your inference.
  • Avoid the following verbs: to show, to portray, to tell, to illustrate, to depict, to inform.

flashcards.q: How many marks are Inference with Purpose questions worth?
flashcards.a: 7 marks.

flashcards.q: How much time should be spent on this question type?
flashcards.a: About 10-12 minutes, but no more.

flashcards.q: What is another name for Inference with Purpose questions?
flashcards.a: 'Why' questions.

flashcards.q: Give an example of an Inference with Purpose question.
flashcards.a: "Why was this cartoon published?" or "What is the intention of the cartoonist in publishing this source?"

flashcards.q: How many paragraphs are needed for this answer if well written?
flashcards.a: One paragraph will suffice if well written and elaborated upon.

flashcards.q: Give a good starting sentence for this answer type.
flashcards.a: "The source was published to influence/educate/persuade/criticise/justify..."

flashcards.q: What verbs should you avoid using when describing the cartoonist's purpose?
flashcards.a: To show, to portray, to tell, to illustrate, to depict, to inform.

flashcards.q: Why should you avoid the verbs 'to show, to portray, to tell, to illustrate, to depict, to inform'?
flashcards.a: Because they describe content rather than convey the source's actual persuasive purpose/intention.

quiz.question: How many marks is an Inference with Purpose ('Why') question worth?
quiz.explanation: The notes state this question type is worth 7 marks.

quiz.question: Which verb would be appropriate to open an Inference with Purpose answer?
quiz.explanation: The notes list 'to show, to portray, to tell, to illustrate, to depict, to inform' as verbs to avoid; 'to persuade' is given as an example appropriate opening verb.

quiz.question: What is another name for this question type?
quiz.explanation: The notes state Inference with Purpose questions are also known as 'Why' questions.

quiz.question: How many paragraphs are typically needed for a well-written answer to this question type?
choices: One paragraph, if well written and elaborated
quiz.explanation: The notes state one paragraph will suffice if well written and elaborated upon.

quiz.question: Why should verbs like 'to show' or 'to depict' be avoided?
choices: They merely describe rather than convey purpose/intention
quiz.explanation: These verbs describe content rather than the persuasive intention behind the source, which is the focus of a purpose question.

shortAnswer.prompt: Explain how to structure an answer to an Inference with Purpose ('Why') question, including what to avoid.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: An Inference with Purpose answer can be a single well-elaborated paragraph, starting with a sentence like 'The source was published to influence/educate/persuade/criticise/justify...' As with plain inference questions, you should not repeat words found in the source and should avoid one-word inferences. Crucially, avoid verbs such as 'to show, to portray, to tell, to illustrate, to depict, to inform' since these describe content rather than convey the cartoonist's actual intention or purpose.
rubric: Notes one paragraph can suffice if well elaborated
Gives an appropriate purpose-oriented starting sentence
States avoidance of source-word repetition and one-word inferences
Lists the prohibited descriptive verbs and explains why

topics.title: Comparison
topics.notesHtml:
Types of Questions

  • How similar/how different are the sources?
  • To what extent do the sources agree with Hitler?
  • How far do the sources agree on the League of Nations?

Structure

3 Paragraphs

  1. First and Second Paragraph - One paragraph on 'agree' and another on 'disagree' (whether similarity or difference comes first depends on what the question asks for first).
    • Basis of comparison/overarching statement: e.g. Sources B and C agree that the peacekeepers enforced a harsh peace settlement on Germany/dictated peace/did not invite Germany to the negotiations.
    • Message: source evidence + inference (evidence must match/support the basis of comparison).
  2. Third Paragraph
    • Agree or disagree based on the purpose and perspective of the source, with support of source provenance.
    • Must include purpose and outcome as well as the audience in relation to both sources' perspective of the issue.
    • Ideally, compare the audience outcome and the purpose. However, if the audience outcome is too generic (e.g. so that the British can understand the situation), focus instead on comparing the speaker's intention.
    • Purpose has to focus on the verb used (refer to Inference with Purpose), and show how it impacts as well as the change in the audience.

Example (Treaty of Versailles): both sources disagree - one is to criticise the Allies, in hopes that the Allies will reconsider the terms; the other is to justify the terms, in hopes that people will find it fair.

Example starting sentence: "Sources B and C agree..."

Note: use the exact word given in the question - if it says 'similar', use 'similar'/'different', not 'agree'/'disagree'.

Notes

  • [7 Marks] (spend about 10-12 minutes on this question, but no more)
  • Follow the question phrasing exactly.
  • Do not compare descriptions (what the source says) - compare an inference made about the issue, either chosen by yourself or directed by the question (e.g. "To what extent is Source A similar to Source B on its views on the benefits of Hitler's policies" requires an inference on the views on the benefits of Hitler's policies).
  • Answers must start with an overarching idea (a similarity or difference) and then go on to explain each source. Avoid starting like "Source A says... and Source B says..."; instead use a connecting phrase like "Source A and Source B differ on..."
  • Do not simply quote the sources - provide ample explanation after each quote to show similarity or difference.
  • Do not assume all sources share a similarity or difference in tone. There is no such phrase as 'neutral tone' - the comparison of tone will always be different.

flashcards.a: 7 marks.

flashcards.q: How much time should be spent on a Comparison question?
flashcards.a: About 10-12 minutes, but no more.

flashcards.q: How many paragraphs does the Comparison structure have?
flashcards.a: 3 paragraphs.

flashcards.a: One paragraph on 'agree' and another on 'disagree' (order depends on what the question asks for first).

flashcards.a: The evidence must match/support the basis of comparison (overarching statement).

flashcards.q: What does the third paragraph of a Comparison answer focus on?
flashcards.a: Agree or disagree based on the purpose and perspective of the source, supported by source provenance, including audience and outcome.

flashcards.q: What should you compare if the audience outcome is too generic?
flashcards.a: Focus instead on comparing the speaker's intention.

flashcards.q: What is a good starting sentence for a Comparison answer?
flashcards.a: "Sources B and C agree..."

flashcards.q: If the question uses the word 'similar' rather than 'agree', what should you do?
flashcards.a: Use the exact word given in the question - 'similar'/'different' instead of 'agree'/'disagree'.

flashcards.q: What should you compare instead of merely comparing what the sources say (descriptions)?
flashcards.a: Compare an inference made about the issue, either chosen by yourself or directed by the question.

flashcards.q: How should you begin a Comparison answer, structurally?
flashcards.a: Start with an overarching idea (a similarity or difference), not by simply stating 'Source A says... and Source B says...'

flashcards.q: Is there such a thing as a 'neutral tone' comparison?
flashcards.a: No - there is no such phrase as 'neutral tone'; the comparison of tone will always be different.

shortAnswer.prompt: Outline the three-paragraph structure for answering a Comparison question.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: The first two paragraphs cover agreement and disagreement respectively (order depends on the question), each starting with a basis of comparison/overarching statement, followed by source evidence and inference that matches this basis. The third paragraph compares the sources' purpose and perspective, supported by source provenance, considering the audience, outcome, and the speaker's intention in relation to both sources' perspectives on the issue - if the audience outcome is too generic, focus on comparing the speaker's intention instead.

Notes evidence must match/support the basis of comparison

shortAnswer.prompt: Explain two common mistakes to avoid when answering a Comparison question.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: First, avoid comparing mere descriptions of what each source says; instead compare an inference made about the issue. Second, avoid starting paragraphs with 'Source A says... and Source B says...'; instead begin with an overarching idea of similarity or difference, using a connecting phrase such as 'Source A and Source B differ on...'. Additionally, do not simply quote sources without explanation, and remember tone comparisons are never 'neutral' - they will always differ.
rubric: Identifies avoiding description-only comparison in favour of inference comparison
Identifies avoiding the 'Source A says...Source B says' opening
Mentions providing explanation after quotes, not just quoting
Mentions there is no 'neutral tone' comparison

topics.title: Reliability
topics.notesHtml:
Types of Questions

  • How reliable is Source A?
  • To what extent can Source A be trusted?
  • To what extent is Source A reliable?
  • Do you believe Source A?

Other Possible Questions

  • Credible
  • Trustworthy
  • Believe
  • Prove
  • Accept

Structure

3 Paragraphs. Either 2 paragraphs on 'reliable' and one on 'not reliable', or vice versa (rarely all reliable or all not reliable). Use the exact word given in the question (e.g. if 'trustworthy' is used, use 'trustworthy' not 'reliable').

  1. First Paragraph
    • Answer the question by making an inference with source content (e.g. Source A is reliable as it shows that Hitler disliked the Jews).
    • Using source evidence, provide a quotation or description of the source to support your inference.
    • Elaborate on your quotation/description to support your inference and answer the question.
    • Link your explanation back to the question - reliable or not reliable.
  2. Second Paragraph
    • Answer the question by cross-referencing to contextual knowledge (e.g. Source A is reliable as, according to context, Hitler did indeed dislike the Jews, so the source/inference is supported by contextual knowledge).
    • Explain.
    • Link back by stating "Thus, Source A is reliable" or "Thus, Source A has limited reliability."
  3. Third Paragraph
    • Answer the question through a closer examination of the provenance and purpose of the source.
    • Start with the speaker's intention and explain (use purposed verbs, refer to Inference with Purpose; the purpose must focus on the verb used and show how it impacts and changes the audience).
    • Show the speaker's context/situation (based on provenance - the year or context in which the source was published, or the writer) and explain.
    • Explain the bias (if any), reasons to be one-sided in an argument (if any), and the position of the speaker (unbiased or biased).
    • Link back to answer the question (e.g. "Thus, Source A is ultimately unreliable").

Note: Useful words/phrases for tone and perspective include 'unbiased', 'objective', 'subjective', 'biased', 'official', and 'exaggerated to an extent where what it depicts may not necessarily be true and reliable.' Always note that meeting minutes or official documents are objective and unbiased.

Example starting sentence: "Source A is not reliable/reliable as..."

Notes

  • [8 Marks] (spend about 10-12 minutes on this question, but no more)
  • Always repeat the keyword used in the question (e.g. if 'believe' is used, use 'believe' in your answer, not 'reliable').
  • Must include purpose and outcome as well as the audience in relation to both sources' perspective of the issue. Do not simply state that the source remains useful based on its purpose - state what that purpose is.

shortAnswer.prompt: Describe the three-paragraph structure for answering a Reliability question.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Paragraph one makes an inference from the source's content, supported by a quotation or description and elaboration, linking back to whether the source is reliable or not. Paragraph two cross-references this inference to contextual knowledge - if supported, the source is reliable; if not, it has limited reliability - and links back accordingly. Paragraph three closely examines the source's provenance and purpose: the speaker's intention (using purpose verbs), the speaker's context/situation, and any bias or one-sidedness, before linking back to a final judgement on reliability, considering audience and outcome in relation to both sources' perspective of the issue.

topics.title: Usefulness
topics.notesHtml:
Types of Questions

  • How useful is Source A as evidence about Hitler using terror on the Germans?
  • How useful is Source A as evidence about the Policy of Appeasement?

Structure

3 Paragraphs. Either 2 paragraphs on 'useful' and one on 'not useful', or vice versa (rarely entirely useful or completely not useful).

  1. First Paragraph
    • Answer the question by making an inference with source content (e.g. Source A is useful in showing how the Jews were mistreated by Hitler).
    • Using source evidence, provide a quotation or description to support your inference.
    • Elaborate on your quotation/description to support your inference and answer the question.
    • Link your explanation back to the question - useful or not useful.
  2. Second Paragraph
    • Answer the question by cross-referencing to contextual knowledge (e.g. Source A is useful as, according to context, the Jews were indeed mistreated by Hitler, so the source/inference is supported by contextual knowledge).
    • Explain.
    • Link back by stating "Thus, Source A is useful" or "Thus, Source A has limited usefulness."
    • Also list the limitations of the source (e.g. "Source A only discusses one reason as to why the Policy of Appeasement was adopted, which is the fear of communism. However, it does not cover other reasons such as the need for time to rearm or the need to protect their economies and colonies.")
  3. Third Paragraph
    • Answer the question through a closer examination of the provenance and purpose of the source.
    • Start with the speaker's intention and explain (use purposed verbs, refer to Inference with Purpose; the purpose must focus on the verb used and show how it impacts and changes the audience).
    • Show the speaker's context/situation (based on provenance - year or context in which the source was published, or writer) and explain.
    • Explain the bias (if any), reasons to be one-sided (if any), and the position of the speaker (unbiased or biased).
    • Consider the source's reliability and how usefulness is affected (a source can be unreliable but still useful).
    • Link back to answer the question (e.g. "Thus, Source A is ultimately unreliable").

Note: Useful words/phrases include 'unbiased', 'objective', 'subjective', 'biased', 'official', and 'exaggerated to an extent where what it depicts may not necessarily be true and reliable.' Meeting minutes or official documents are objective and unbiased.

Important: just because a source is not reliable does not mean it is not useful. For example, if the question asks "How useful is this source in highlighting the issues faced by the Weimar Government?" and the source is a propaganda poster by Hitler, the source will clearly be unreliable but still useful, as it still highlights the issues faced.

Example starting sentence: "Source A is not useful/useful as..."

Notes

topics.title: Testing Assertion
topics.notesHtml:
Types of Questions

  • Study all sources. "Hitler was an effective leader." How far do the sources support this statement?
  • Study all the sources. "Hitler's economic policies benefited the lives of the Germans." How far do these sources support this view? Explain your answer using sources and your knowledge.

Structure

First, separate the sources into two categories: 'agree with the statement' and 'disagree with the statement'.

Agree with the statementDisagree with the statement
Source A, Source ESource B, Source C and Source D

Typically, try to make it balanced in a 2:2 ratio, but if not possible, a 2:3 or 3:2 ratio works as well. Even a 3:1 ratio will work. Most of the time, due to time constraints, it is best to work with only 4 sources. You must be clear and accurate about which sources agree and which disagree.

6 Paragraphs:

  1. Source A supports this view... + Source Evidence and Explanation
  2. Source E supports this view... + Source Evidence and Explanation
  3. However, Source B does not support this view... + Source Evidence and Explanation
  4. Source C also does not support this view... + Source Evidence and Explanation
  5. Finally, Source D also does not support this view... + Source Evidence and Explanation
  6. General analysis of the majority of sources (e.g. most of the sources do not support this claim); Context (confirm if the claim is accurate, and if not, challenge the claim subtly - only include this in the final paragraph, not at the end of every body paragraph, e.g. "In addition, according to context..."); Link back to the claim.

Example starting sentence: "Source A supports this view..."

Notes

topics.title: Hybrid Reliability - With a Primary Source
topics.notesHtml:
Types of Questions

Does Source A prove that Source B is wrong about Hitler's rule? (There is a primary source - Source A)

Big Idea

Involves the critical analysis of the reliability of one source using another source. The skills are very much like reliability, but involve the use of more than one source.

Structure

3 Paragraphs. Either 2 paragraphs on 'can prove wrong' and one on 'cannot prove wrong', or vice versa (rarely entirely one or the other).

  1. First Paragraph
    • Present an overarching idea with the comparison (look for a similarity or difference in content) - make an inference of both sources and compare the inferences to see if they say the same or different things.
    • Using source evidence, provide a quotation or description to support your comparison.
    • Elaborate on your quotation/description to support your inference and answer the question.
    • Link back to the question - can prove wrong or cannot prove wrong.
    • If the source content is similar -> cannot prove wrong/reliable. If the source content is different -> can prove wrong/not reliable.
  2. Second Paragraph
    • Cross-reference the main source to contextual knowledge (e.g. "Upon cross-referencing Source A to contextual knowledge, Source A can prove Source B wrong..."). Source A has to be reliable in order to prove something.
    • If context matches -> Source A is factually accurate and supported by context, meaning Source A is reliable and will continue to either prove wrong or cannot prove wrong (refer to first paragraph).
    • If context does not match -> Source A is proven wrong, factually inaccurate, lacks credibility, and thus cannot prove anything.
    • Summary table: If Paragraph 1 found sources similar in inference (cannot prove wrong) and CK matches -> cannot prove wrong; if CK does not match -> cannot prove anything. If Paragraph 1 found sources different in inference (can prove wrong) and CK matches -> can prove wrong; if CK does not match -> cannot prove anything.
    • Explain, then link back stating "Thus, Source A can prove Source B wrong" or "Thus, Source A cannot prove Source B wrong."
  3. Third Paragraph
    • Closer examination of the provenance and purpose of the source.
    • Start with the speaker's intention and explain (use purposed verbs, refer to Inference with Purpose).
    • Show the speaker's context/situation (based on provenance) and explain.
    • Explain bias (if any), reasons to be one-sided (if any), and the position of the speaker.
    • Consider the source's reliability: if found unbiased/reliable upon analysing purpose and provenance -> Source A can prove Source B wrong; if found unreliable -> Source A cannot prove Source B wrong.
    • Link back to answer the question (e.g. "Thus, Source A is ultimately unable to prove that Source B is wrong").
    • Even if Source A was originally similar in content to Source B, the focus is on the reliability and usefulness of Source A in its ability to prove Source B wrong, not simply a content match.
    • Bring in the CAP (Content, Author/Attitude, Purpose) of the secondary source if it affects the CAP of the primary source (e.g. if both sources are opponents, they cannot prove each other wrong; there is no need to explicitly do the CAP of the secondary source, just state that they are opponents).

Note: Useful words/phrases include 'unbiased', 'objective', 'subjective', 'biased', 'official', and 'exaggerated to an extent where what it depicts may not necessarily be true and reliable.' Meeting minutes or official documents are objective and unbiased.

Example starting sentence: "Source A can prove that Source B is wrong about Hitler's rule as..."

Mark Scheme

LevelDescriptionMarks
L1Use of source details with no reference to the question[1]
L2/3Similarity/Difference in the sources (Step 1)[2-3]
L3/4Reliability of Source A using contextual knowledge (Step 2)[4-5]
L5Establishing the credibility of Source A through critical analysis of its provenance (Step 3)[6-7]

[7 Marks]

Important Notes

  • Always answer the question - your opening sentence per paragraph may differ based on the question (e.g. it may be "can/cannot prove that Source B is right" or "can/cannot justify that Source B is wrong", not only "can/cannot prove wrong"). Make sure your opening sentence answers the actual question asked.
  • Analyse the sources carefully.
  • The opening sentence/conclusion for each paragraph/source can differ - e.g. Paragraph 1: Source A can prove Source B wrong; Paragraph 2: Source A cannot prove Source B wrong; Paragraph 3: Source A cannot prove Source B wrong. This is acceptable and does not need to be consistent throughout.

topics.title: Hybrid Reliability - No Primary Source
topics.notesHtml:
Types of Questions

Can you trust Source A more than Source B? (There is NO primary source)

Big Idea

Involves the critical analysis of the reliability of one source using another source. The skills are very much like reliability, involving the use of more than one source.

Structure

3 Paragraphs. Either 2 paragraphs on 'can prove wrong' and one on 'cannot prove wrong', or vice versa (rarely entirely one or the other).

  1. First Paragraph
    • Present an overarching idea with the comparison (look for a similarity or difference in content).
    • Using source evidence, provide a quotation or description to support your comparison.
    • Elaborate to support your inference and answer the question.
    • Link back - can prove wrong or cannot prove wrong.
    • If the source content is similar -> cannot trust Source A more. If the source content is different -> can trust Source A more.
  2. Second Paragraph
    • Cross-reference both sources to contextual knowledge (e.g. "Upon cross-referencing Source A to contextual knowledge, Source A is supported by contextual knowledge while Source B is not, hence Source A is more reliable, so you can trust Source A more.")
    • If context supports Source A but not Source B -> can trust Source A more (vice versa for Source B). If context does not support either source -> cannot trust anything (Source A) (unlikely scenario).
    • Explain, then link back by stating "Thus, Source A can prove Source B wrong" or "Thus, Source A cannot prove Source B wrong."
  3. Third Paragraph
    • Closer examination of the provenance and purpose of the source, doing a critical analysis of both sources.
    • Start with the speaker's intention and explain (use purposed verbs).
    • Show the speaker's context/situation (based on provenance) and explain.
    • Explain bias (if any), reasons to be one-sided (if any), and the position of the speaker.
    • Consider the source's reliability: if Source A is found unbiased/more reliable upon analysing purpose and provenance -> can trust Source A more; if Source A is found less reliable and Source B more reliable -> cannot trust Source A more.
    • Link back to answer the question (e.g. "Thus, Source A is ultimately unable to prove that Source B is wrong").

Note: Useful words/phrases include 'unbiased', 'objective', 'subjective', 'biased', 'official', and 'exaggerated to an extent where what it depicts may not necessarily be true and reliable.' Meeting minutes or official documents are objective and unbiased.

Example starting sentence: "Source A cannot be trusted more than Source B about Hitler's rule as..."

topics.title: Separate Inference
topics.notesHtml:
Types of Questions

Source A and B differ in their views about Germany. Does it make one of them useless? (Not a strong need for comparison)

Big Idea

Involves the critical analysis of the reliability of one source using another source. The skills are very much like reliability, involving the use of more than one source.

Structure

3 Paragraphs. Either 2 paragraphs on 'can prove wrong' and one on 'cannot prove wrong', or vice versa (rarely entirely one or the other).

  1. First Paragraph - Make an inference from the content of Source A, cross-reference Source A to context, and critically analyse the source's purpose and provenance.
  2. Second Paragraph - Make an inference from the content of Source B, cross-reference Source B to context, and critically analyse the source's purpose and provenance.
  3. Third Paragraph - Analyse what you have found in the first two paragraphs to ascertain which source is useful/useless.

topics.title: Surprised
topics.notesHtml:
Surprised vs Reliability

Judgement for 'Surprised' questions is NOT based on reliability.

StepSurprisedReliability
InferenceABC (use the person's position/context to say why it is surprising - this paragraph is mainly for the inference; no judgement required)ABC (cannot be same wording as the question issue - e.g. for 'Is the source reliable in showing you that the US was to be blamed for the Korean War?', answer: Reliable, as it shows the US was to be blamed because [inference, e.g. the source shows they were overly aggressive])
CR to CKSupport = not surprised (ABC); Challenge = surprised (not ABC)Support = reliable (ABC); Challenge = not reliable (not ABC)
CAPPerson's position + intention (criticise, praise, warn, etc.) + context. If you can understand why the person would say this -> not surprised. If you cannot understand why -> surprised.Person's intention (criticise, praise, warn, etc.) + context -> Is there bias? If you understand the bias using context, it is reliable. If you do not understand the bias using context, it is not reliable. (Bias does not instantly make it unreliable - you must consider the context.) Even in usefulness, if unreliable, check if the inference is still useful: ask how the inference is affected by reliability, and why it might still remain useful despite being biased. If you can justify why it remains useful, it is useful; if not, it is not useful.

Types of Questions

Are you surprised by what Source E says?

Big Idea

  • Similar skill to reliability with similar steps.
  • Essentially and very simply looking at a source's content and seeing if it is contrary to what we commonly know or have learnt.

Structure

3 Paragraphs

  1. First Paragraph
    • Answer the question by making an inference with source content (e.g. Source A is surprising as it suggests that Hitler was kind to the Jews).
    • Using source evidence, provide a quotation or description to support your inference.
    • Elaborate to support your inference and answer the question.
    • Link back - surprising or not surprising.
    • Note: you must always discuss the element of surprise based on the person's position, not just "...is in the source so it means this...so it is surprising" - instead: "...said..., meaning..., so it is surprising."
  2. Second Paragraph
    • Answer the question by cross-referencing to contextual knowledge (e.g. Source A is surprising as, according to context, the Jews were mistreated by Hitler, so the source/inference is challenged by contextual knowledge).
    • Explain, then link back by stating "Thus, Source A is surprising" or "Thus, Source A is not surprising."
    • Note: this paragraph is checking for a content match (not reliability, not a person's position). If the content does not match and challenges the source, it is surprising. If content matches and supports the source, it is not surprising. It is alright for the conclusion to change (e.g. not surprising at the start, but surprising now).
  3. Third Paragraph
    • Closer examination of the provenance and purpose of the source.
    • Start with the speaker's intention and explain (use purposed verbs, refer to Inference with Purpose).
    • Show the speaker's context/situation (based on provenance) and explain.
    • Example: a propaganda poster is not surprising as it is expected to influence the mass public to support (its cause), whereas a photo of a Jew seen praising Hitler is surprising as it is unexpected. (The purpose of a source is surprising only when the purpose presents an outcome contrary to one's expected idea.)
    • Link back to answer the question (e.g. "Thus, Source A is ultimately not surprising") by explaining why you are or are not surprised based on the analysis. If you understand the reasons for the inference (why the source says this), you are not surprised; if you do not understand the reasons, you are surprised.

Note: Useful words/phrases include 'unbiased', 'objective', 'subjective', 'biased', 'official', and 'exaggerated to an extent where what it depicts may not necessarily be true and reliable.' Meeting minutes or official documents are objective and unbiased.

Example starting sentence: "I am surprised/not surprised" or "Source A is surprising/not surprising."

Important Notes

  • Always answer the question - the opening sentence may differ based on the question (e.g. "Is it surprising/not surprising" etc.). Make sure your opening sentence answers the actual question.
  • Analyse the sources carefully.
  • The opening sentence/conclusion for each paragraph can differ - e.g. Paragraph 1: surprising; Paragraph 2: not surprising; Paragraph 3: surprising. This is acceptable and does not need to be consistent throughout.
  • There will always be a surprising element in the question.

topics.title: Surprised with 2 Sources
topics.notesHtml:
Types of Questions

Having read Source A, are you surprised about Source B?

Big Idea

Similar skills and steps to 'Are you surprised' questions with 2 sources, as well as hybrid skills.

Structure

First, identify the main source (the primary source you look at):

QuestionMain Source
Does Source A make you surprised about Source B?Source B
Having read Source B, are you surprised about Source A?Source A

3 Paragraphs

  1. First Paragraph - Compare the sources and look for similarities or differences.
    • If content is similar/both sources share similar views/perspectives -> not surprised by the main source after reading the other source.
    • If content is different/sources differ in views/perspectives -> surprised by the main source after reading the other source.
    • Substantiate your claim with evidence and elaboration from both sources to show the similarity or difference.
  2. Second Paragraph - Cross-reference the main source with contextual knowledge, with minor attention given to the other source.
    • If main source is supported by contextual knowledge -> not surprised by the main source, as it is not entirely reliable when considering contextual knowledge (careful: it is still framed as not surprised because it's internally consistent/supported).
    • If main source is not supported by contextual knowledge -> surprised by the main source.
    • Substantiate your claim with contextual knowledge and elaboration. Give minor attention to the other source (a short sentence justifying its reliability), e.g. "Source F comes from President Truman, an official point of view, and thus after reading Source F which is most likely reliable, I am surprised by Source E as Source E itself is not entirely reliable based on my contextual knowledge."
  3. Third Paragraph - Check the reliability of the main source based on its purpose and provenance, with minor attention given to the other source.
    • If the other source has a more objective purpose (less likely to have ulterior motives) while the main source is more biased (more likely to have other intentions) -> surprised by the main source, as it itself is not reliable based on closer analysis of its purpose and provenance, while the other source is more reliable.
    • If the main source has a more objective purpose while the other source is more biased -> not surprised by the main source, as it is more reliable based on closer analysis, while the other source is not as reliable.
    • Substantiate your claim with purpose, provenance and elaboration.

Example starting sentence: "After reading Source F, I am surprised/not surprised..."

Important Notes

  • Always answer the question - opening sentences may vary (e.g. "Is it surprising/not surprising"). Make sure your opening sentence answers the actual question.
  • Analyse the sources carefully.
  • The opening sentence/conclusion for each paragraph can differ across paragraphs and this is acceptable.

topics.title: Hybrid Surprised
topics.notesHtml:
Types of Questions

Does Source A make you surprised about Source B?

Big Idea

Similar skill to comparison and hybrid reliability questions with similar steps.

Structure

First, identify the main source (the primary source):

QuestionMain Source
Does Source A make you surprised about Source B?Source A

Note: although this uses similar skills/steps to 'Are you surprised' questions with 2 sources, they are distinct question types:

  • 'Are you surprised' questions with 2 sources (e.g. "Having read Source A, are you surprised by Source B") - main source is Source B; think of it as focusing on the effect.
  • Hybrid surprise questions (e.g. "Does Source A make you surprised about Source B") - main source is Source A; think of it as focusing on the cause.

3 Paragraphs

  1. First Paragraph - Compare the sources and look for similarities or differences.
    • If content is similar/both sources share similar views/perspectives -> not surprised by the main source.
    • If content is different/sources differ in views/perspectives -> surprised by the main source.
    • Substantiate your claim with evidence and elaboration, providing evidence from both sources.
  2. Second Paragraph - Cross-reference the main source with contextual knowledge.
    • If main source is supported by contextual knowledge -> the main source does make me feel surprised by the other source, as the main source is in itself a reliable source when considering contextual knowledge.
    • If main source is not supported by contextual knowledge -> the main source does not make me feel surprised by the other source, as the main source is in itself an unreliable source when considering contextual knowledge.
    • Substantiate with contextual knowledge and elaboration. Unlike 'Are you surprised' questions with 2 sources, there is no need to pay minor attention to the other source here.
  3. Third Paragraph - Check the purposes and context of BOTH sources (another differing point from 'Are you surprised' questions with 2 sources).
    • Using intention and context: if you can understand why the sources are similar, you are not surprised. If you can understand why they are different, you are also not surprised.
    • If you cannot understand why they are similar, you are surprised. If you cannot understand why they are different, you remain surprised.

Example starting sentence: "(Main source) does/does not make me feel surprised by (other source)..."

Notes

  • Always answer the question.
  • Analyse the sources carefully and identify the right main source.
  • Be careful not to confuse these questions with 'Are you surprised' questions with 2 sources.
  • The opening sentence/conclusion for each paragraph can differ across paragraphs and this is acceptable.

topics.title: Essay: Key Notes and Overview of Skills
topics.notesHtml:
Key Definitions

  • Social transformation - changes in political, economic, social, and cultural structures in society.
  • Social identity - essential qualities that determine membership in a certain social group (something that defines you and what you do).
  • Social identity creation - a process of redefining the essential qualities of membership in a particular group and seeking legitimisation of this definition (i.e. "No, this is who I want to be instead and how I want to be treated in society now, please accept me").

Important Pointers for Writing Essays

  • Directly answer the question and signpost ('link') each paragraph to the question. Avoid strongly focusing on comparing just because it is a comparative essay, and thereby failing to answer the question.
  • Provide ample substantiation and/or discuss competing perspectives in detail.
  • Include concrete details, context and explanations so it is clear why a factor was a driving force (evidence is important but need not be overly specific).

Overview of Essay Skills

Overall Guiding Questions for Essays

  1. What were the major forces and developments during this period?
  2. What caused these major forces and developments?
  3. Who were the key players involved?
  4. How did the developments influence people's decisions and actions, and vice versa?
  5. How did people's views and perspectives shape their interpretation of these developments?
  6. How did these developments impact societies?

Overall Guiding Rules for Essays

  1. Identify the factor in the question (e.g. the need to create a new social identity), usually flagged by a weighing word like 'most', 'key', or 'primarily driven'.
  2. Answer the question - address the given factor/reason first and state your argument for why it is a factor.
  3. Pump in content knowledge to back up your argument.
  4. Answer why the chosen factor is more important than the other factors.
  5. Time given: 1 hour 30 minutes (spend roughly 45 minutes on each essay, no more than 45 minutes each). 3 questions are given, of which Question 1 is compulsory, and you choose 1 of Question 2 or Question 3 - you must know your case studies well.

topics.title: Level 1 Essay Questions
topics.notesHtml:
Extreme/Relative Importance Questions

Example questions: "Assess which term of the Treaty of Versailles was the most unreasonable." / "'The reason for the start of WWII in Europe was due to XYZ.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer." (i.e. questions asking for the most unreasonable/most important reason)

  1. Identify the factor in the question (e.g. the need to create a new social identity), usually with a weighing word like 'most', 'key', 'primarily driven'.
  2. Answer the question - address the given factor/reason first and state your argument for why it is a factor.
  3. Pump in content knowledge to back up your argument.
  4. Answer why the chosen factor is more important than the other two factors (requires weighing).

Balanced Perspective Questions

Example questions: "'War is inevitable.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer." / "Assess the importance of XYZ in the outcome of the civil movements in the USA." / "'X is more Yes than No for Y.' How far do you agree? Explain your answer."

  1. Identify the factor in the question, usually with a weighing word like 'most', 'key', 'primarily driven'.
  2. Answer the question - address the given factor/reason first and state your argument for why it is a factor.
  3. Pump in content knowledge to back up your argument.
  4. NEVER use a hypothetical situation (especially for questions on whether war was inevitable).
  5. Answer why both sides can happen (provide a balanced perspective).

Structure

  • Introduction: Short, about 3-4 lines - briefly discuss the issue the question raises and what your essay is about.
  • 3 Body Paragraphs
    • Point: must be specific (e.g. Discrimination -> Education, not just 'discrimination').
    • Evidence: a case study (an event, or an action taken by a group of people/single person - just 1, with an adequate description of relevant information, 4-5 lines).
    • Elaboration: link the information of the case study to the point.
    • Link: link the point made in the entire body paragraph to the question.
  • Conclusion: reiterate your stand and evaluate your points using a basis of comparison (e.g. long term vs short term, or extent).

topics.title: Comparative Essay Questions
topics.notesHtml:
Overall Guiding Rules for Comparative Essays

  1. Identify that the question requires you to use 2 case studies to support your argument (you need to make a judgement - choosing similarities/differences, or choosing case studies to illustrate your argument).
  2. Answer the question through: (a) content match - comparison of reasons, cause and effect, impact/consequence; (b) analysis based on criterion - social/political/economic, country, situation, people, government.

Direct Compare and Contrast Questions

Example questions: "Compare and contrast any 2 conflicts in the Cold War." / "Compare and contrast any two Cold War conflicts and their impacts." / "Compare and contrast any two Cold War conflicts and their causes."

Comparison is important - need to show explicit similarities and differences (choosing similarities and differences). Possible comparative topics: power and authority; reasons for the rise to power; policies for the control of people/consolidation of power/securing power; impact of the dictatorship.

Structure

  • Introduction: include a short context about the case studies and the question, and a thesis statement that answers the question and lists your arguments.
  • 3 Body Paragraphs: Point (answering the question - either a similarity or difference in a specific area); Evidence (relevant details about both conflicts to highlight the similarity/difference); Elaboration (elaborate and explain how details show the similarity/difference); Link (link the point back to answering the main question).
  • Conclusion: short conclusion to reiterate your stand and evaluate the similarities and differences/provide additional comments, going back to answer the question.

Evaluative Comparative Questions

Example questions: "Assess if social movements in Southeast Asia were valid. Use 2 case studies from the period of 1970s to 2000s to illustrate your argument." / "Evaluate the impact of social transformations in Southeast Asia. Use the case studies of at least 2 countries to support your argument."

No need for explicit comparison (choosing case studies to illustrate your argument). The idea is to illustrate an argument using 2 case studies.

Key Things in an Evaluative Comparative Essay

Content match:

  • When comparing the 2 case studies, be careful not to just list a chunk of information.
  • Avoid simply comparing similarities and differences.
  • Instead, compare with varying criteria and perspectives - can compare causes and effects, or things of different values like extent or methods.

Analysis:

  • Throughout the entire essay, there should be relevant analysis.
  • Use comparisons to build an argument that answers the question.

Structure

  • Introduction: include a short context about the case studies and the question (e.g. context about what social movements in Southeast Asia were, or gender roles, plus short context about case studies like the Free Aceh Movement). Include a thesis statement that answers the question and lists your arguments - by comparing the content/case studies, it should form an argument that ultimately answers the question (e.g. "It is not valid as both the Free Aceh Movement and People Power Movement are similar in reflecting that...").
  • 3 Body Paragraphs: Point (a similarity or difference in a specific area); Evidence (relevant, sufficient details about both conflicts); Elaboration (explain how details show the similarity/difference); Link (link back to the main question).
  • Conclusion: short conclusion reiterating your stand, evaluating similarities/differences or providing additional comments, going back to answer the question.

Criteria and Perspectives for Comparison

CriterionPerspective
TimeShort-term/Long-term (relate to a focus area, e.g. impact/effects)
TimeImmediate/Future
TimePeace time/During a crisis
TimeStart of the movement/During a movement/At the end of a movement
Areas of influenceSocial/Political/Economic
PeopleHigh income/Low income; Rich/Poor; Government/Citizens; Supporters/Condemned
Stages of causationRoot cause/Trigger cause
ApproachIntention/Method used; Violent/Peaceful; Gradual/Intentional
ImpactLong term/Short term
FocusCountry's needs/People's needs

On the 'Start/During/End of movement' perspective: consider the development of social movements or changes in gender roles, and how different parties played a role in the development (e.g. the involvement of the Catholic Church). Consider the various turning points in the movement, how it changed, the impacts and effects of various parties' involvement at different stages, and the effect of these actions on the parties themselves.

On the 'Gradual/Intentional' perspective: consider the process of social movements and change in gender roles, and the differences between social transformation, social transitions and social movements. Consider whether these changes were expected and part of a gradual, natural change across the world, or intentional movements specific to countries.

  • Social movements - deliberate and intentional changes that people move and act towards (e.g. Free Aceh Movement and People Power Movement).
  • Social transformations - not forced, and change over time from one period to another.
  • Social transitions - a quicker-paced transition, whereby a sudden change occurs in an instant or over a few days.

Show contrasting perspectives.

topics.title: General Points to Note (Exam Technique)
topics.notesHtml:
1. Always do some preparation before writing your answer

  • Read the question and its "provenance" — the text above the question or the data given may prove useful in helping you understand the question and answer it better.
  • Plan the points you intend to write in your answer, taking note of the pointers below as you plan.
  • Always read the question itself carefully. For example, if the question says "using the sequence identified in the diagram", then you must use that sequence. So besides being alert to understand the question, you must also respect the question context and answer it accurately.

2. Always pay attention to mark allocation to know how much to write

[4] and [6] mark questions can also be known as [2+2] and [3+3] questions respectively. When marks are allocated as such, refer to the table below:

[2+2] questions[3+3] questions
2 points3 points
2 explanations3 explanations

Knowing this, you then know you are not to write too much or too little — bearing in mind that the above only applies when marks are allocated as [2+2] or [3+3]. In all other cases, where marks are allocated as [4] or [6], 4 or 6 points respectively with explanations are required.

Exception: when [4] marks are awarded, there are typically 4 points required to be attained (usually), but in some abnormal cases where only 3 points can be found, it is best to explain as thoroughly as possible so as to avoid the loss of the 4th mark.

3. Always give a variety of answers

Whenever you answer a question involving the keywords below, always remember to give a diversity of answers, because you do not want a situation where, for a push and pull factor question, you simply write "less traffic congestion in MEDC, but more traffic congestion in LEDC". This only warrants 1 mark because you are simply repeating the same point in a different way. Offering a diversity of answers also shows your understanding and may help you attain marks for not-so-complete answers.

KeywordHow to answer
Compare / Compare and ContrastGive both similarities and differences. Also look generally and not too specifically, because a very narrow comparison shows a lack of understanding.
ContrastDifferences only.
Impacts / BenefitsPositive and Negative; use ESPN (Economic, Social, Political, Natural/environmental).
Factors / ReasonsFor factor questions, always try to give push and pull factors. Likewise for reason and factor questions, always give answers based on ESPN, looking at the question from all aspects and not just social or economic factors.
ImpactsFor impact questions, always try to give both positive and negative impacts. If you are very sure there is only one type (either only positive or only negative), then once again give your answers based on ESPN.

topics.title: Data Response Questions (Command Words)
topics.notesHtml:
Command wordHow to answerPoints to noteMarks awarded
State / Identify / Give a reasonJust give the reason or state; no need for explanation, but occasionally requires data from the question.NIL[1–2]
Calculate / DefineJust calculate or define; no need for data or explanation.NIL[1–2]
Describe / SuggestState what you see and give data from the question.Be careful not to start comparing or to start simply stating when you see the word "describe". For example, in a question asking to "describe the growth of cities in the LEDCs and MEDCs", be careful not to compare LEDC and MEDC growth together — instead describe each. Describing is not comparing, but it is also not simply stating: describing something is to use what you see to make an inference (e.g. if a photo of a squatter settlement is given, you cannot just say there is "poor infrastructure" — you must state that "due to the presence of housing made of zinc roofs and iron sheets standing on wood stilts, it shows that there are poor housing structures/poor infrastructure"). When the question asks you to "describe the changes" and provides data, it is important not just to state the data as evidence but to interpret the data. To process data is to give an analysis of the data instead of simply stating it, such as giving percentages to show a rate of change (taken from two extremes, A and B → (B−A)/A × 100% = rate of change in %), as well as using adjectives to describe change (e.g. slight increase, exponential growth, etc.). Should a diagram or data representation (e.g. table, graph, values, photos) be given, the answer must always make reference to it. You must give specific, accurate and relevant data to support your answer. Descriptions/explanations should always be complete, and must always begin with a general statement that directs the answer or directly answers the question. They must also end with a concluding statement that links back to the question.[2–4] (mark allocation may differ — refer above)
Explain / Account forGive data from the question and show what the data tells us with respect to the question.If the question asks to explain with the aid of a well-annotated diagram, refer to the Diagram Sketching section. If the question asks to support your explanation with an example, the example should be at least 2 sentences and must have some details with specific numbers. Should a diagram or data representation (e.g. table, graph, values, photos) be given, the answer must always make reference to it. You must give specific, accurate and relevant data to support your answer. Descriptions/explanations should always be complete, and must always begin with a general statement that directs the answer or directly answers the question, and must end with a concluding statement that links back to the question.[4–6] (mark allocation may differ — refer above)
Compare / Differentiate / ContrastMake a comparison between 2 objects; see the number of marks to determine the number of points and level of explanation.When making a comparison between two different objects, always find a common criteria between them to compare them both.[4–6] (mark allocation may differ — refer above)

Note: When answering the question, should there be details provided by the question (e.g. names of places, certain labels, etc.), these details must be used in the answer.

KeywordHow to answer
Change/GrowthGive data from the question, state the general trend, before and after, cluster, and state anomalies (if any) or highest and lowest.
RelationshipState whether it is a direct or inverse relationship and provide data to show the relationship.
With reference to...Always remember to give data when you see this phrase.
DistributionGive a general trend first, then proceed to cluster (based on what the question gives you — e.g. if the question gives you trenches, cluster based on trenches, not coastal or inland), and finally state anomalies (if any).
Differences...If asked to explain differences, state these differences like how you would compare, except this time you do not state similarities. After stating the differences and showing comparison, explain each of these differences. However, if the question only asks you to state the differences, then just state them.
DifferentiateMust establish a Basis of Comparison, defined as the overarching idea as to why there is a difference.

topics.title: Diagram Sketching
topics.notesHtml:
There are many diagrams you need to be able to sketch, and you need to be able to differentiate between the various types of questions asking you to sketch a diagram.

Types of possible questions

There are three main types of questions they can ask:

  • A well-labelled diagram
  • An annotated diagram
  • "With the aid of a well-labelled diagram, explain the…" (e.g. formation of volcanic island arcs)

Approach to diagram sketching questions

  1. Identify the diagram you need to sketch and then proceed to sketch it.
    • A well-labelled diagram only requires a sketch and simple labelling, so just label the parts of your sketch.
    • An annotated diagram requires a sketch and a short description for each label/part in the sketch. Unless provided with the case below, you do not need to write a paragraph — simply annotate on your sketch and provide a short description of the features.
    • If asked, "With the aid of a well-labelled diagram, account for the formation of stratovolcanoes," you should label a sketched diagram with numbers and then write the process corresponding to the numbers in a paragraph below your sketched and numbered diagram.
  2. Check that you have included all important details in your sketch and drawing. For example, if the question already gives you certain information like the names of places, you must draw and label the plates or include these names of places. Fundamentally, if you are given any information to sketch a diagram, your sketch must show details of the information given to you.

Types of diagrams you need to know how to sketch

  • Convectional rain formation
  • Monsoon diagrams

topics.title: Infographic Analysis
topics.notesHtml:
This section will be worth 10 marks, and can ask a range of questions under this section, by simply providing an infographic.

Types of possible questions

  • Questions asking you to retrieve data from the infographic, e.g.:
    • What is the epicentre?
    • Where is the depth of focus?
    • What are 3 villages affected?
    • Define…
    • State…
  • Questions asking you to analyse the infographic — this means taking data from the infographic and making inferences or explaining and building upon it, instead of just picking it out or stating it. Possible questions include:
    • Suggest why there were so many aftershocks for the 2015 Nepal Earthquake.
    • Describe how the 2015 Nepal Earthquake has affected the economy.

Approach to infographic analysis questions

  1. Read and spend time analysing the infographic, taking note of all the details given to you.
  2. Answer accordingly and always remember that every answer must use the data, including names, figures, maps, images, information, etc.
  3. Do not be careless in analysing the infographic.

Infographics also have different types, with advantages and disadvantages to different types of data representation (refer to the Handout on Graphical Skills).

topics.title: Essay Writing
topics.notesHtml:
Unpacking the question

  • Look at the question and identify the issue.
  • If you see the phrase "To what extent" or "How far", you must:
    1. Take a stand (your thoughts or opinion on the issue and where you stand. Note that your stand can either be to agree to a large extent or a small extent, but not to totally agree or fully disagree).
    2. Consider the merits and perspectives of the argument or concept and discuss/show perspectives (since you cannot totally agree or fully disagree, you must take into account different perspectives — most of the time, 2 perspectives on an issue).
  • After looking at the question, look at the statement and identify keywords. Understand and define these keywords and identify the extreme word, which will tell you where this statement stands or what it is saying on the issue.

Example

Question: To what extent is climate change a threat?
Issue: Climate change
Identify keywords: "To what extent" and "threat"
Define keywords: (i) "To what extent" means we must take a stand and show perspectives. (ii) "Threat" means we are looking at the negative effects — the threats, challenges and risks of climate change.

Essay preparation: (i) The given factor is: climate change is a threat. (ii) The perspectives we can discuss are: climate change is a threat, and climate change is not a threat.

Format

Introduction

  • Begin with a general statement — a broad stroke of what the topic is about (e.g. Migration — across the years, people have been moving across international boundaries in search of a higher standard of living and quality of life).
  • After the general statement, state your scope. Stating your scope is similar to defining terms, but instead of defining the words (e.g. "benefit refers to…"), you are setting boundaries to the keywords (e.g. "Migration has both positive and negative impacts in different aspects, both to the country from where people move from and to where people go to"). Be careful to scope the question correctly (e.g. should the word "today" be used in a question about climate change, it should be narrowed down to global warming). Scoping is a way of narrowing a broad term like climate change and placing it in the right context, not simply defining it.
  • After stating your scope, proceed to the most important part of your introduction — stating your stand. When stating your stand, maintain a more academic perspective and avoid saying "I feel" or "I agree", but rather follow something like: "This statement can be agreed to a small/large extent that (paraphrase the statement if you can, or just copy and paste) as (reasons). However, it must also be acknowledged that (acknowledge the other view)."

Body Paragraph

ComponentGuidance
Topic SentenceBasically, a topic sentence introduces your point. This point should be one key idea, argument or concept, and the topic sentence should state the key idea or concept clearly. Note that the first paragraph/topic sentence must always address the given factor in the question. This sentence should minimally be at least 1 sentence. Keep the topic sentence short — do not repeat "it can be agreed to a large/small extent…" — just get straight to the point and give your reason to justify your stand.
Writing conceptuallyWhile you can continue introducing points, it is important to weave concepts into your arguments and write conceptually. Weaving concepts into your arguments also means substantiating your concepts with evidence and elaboration.
ElaborateAlways use the 5W1H method to expand on your point and explain your key idea or concept in detail and clearly. In particular, ask "how?" and "why?" to elaborate. Think of it as a structured question where you keep linking and making expansions to your point. Always ask why, and offer a step-by-step explanation to prove your point, and make sure your explanation can be supported by evidence. This part should minimally be at least 3 sentences.
EvidenceTo give evidence is simply to give case studies and statistics to support your explanation and point. Always give the strongest and most detailed evidence, and you may adopt the format: (a) name a place, (b) statistics and data, (c) terms. Your case study must also provide relevant information that supports your point (e.g. if your point is that this technology helps minimise impact, state how, like "resist lateral forces, less collapse, less people trapped, less loss of life and destruction to property"). This part should minimally be at least 3 sentences. Ensure you give detailed examples to further illustrate your ideas or concepts — evidence should be specific data (including names, numbers, etc.) and accurate as well as relevant.
EvaluationEvaluation is like a link to close up the paragraph and link everything back to your point and the question (e.g. "Therefore,…"/"As such,…"). This should minimally be at least 1 sentence.

Conclusion/Evaluation

  • Re-emphasise your stand (Basis of Argument — what are you using to prove/justify your stand/what makes it better, e.g. long term vs short term, positive vs negative, cause vs effect, root vs catalyst).
  • Summarise your arguments.
  • Ensure you have given a balanced argument or range of points (2 points for your stand and 1 counterpoint).
  • Present concepts and re-highlight the concepts discussed.

Timing

No more than 25 minutes for 5 paragraphs and planning.

Other notes for Essay

  • Always include case studies but only provide the relevant evidence.
  • Each paragraph must have at least 8 sentences, and your elaboration should be adequate to show a step-by-step link to the point and answer questions like "so?", "how?", "why?".
  • Evidence and explanation must be effective and support your point (e.g. give evidence to show how a country benefits culturally from migration, NOT how a country has racial harmony).
  • Always bear in mind that in the exam you only have 25 minutes, so do not write too much or waste time on unnecessary things like explicitly stating or citing evidence, etc.
  • Do not address two issues or two points in one paragraph.
  • The basis of argument in the conclusion must be clear as to what you are basing it on (impacts? outcomes? — what are you using to show that the host country benefits more?).
  • When introducing a concept, don't be too abrupt — elaborate more rather than touch and go.
  • Do not include examples in the conclusion.
  • Avoid using words like "I", "if", "thus", "hence" or "therefore" (these can be used, but not excessively — only when wrapping up something).
  • There is no fixed structure for an essay, but ultimately you must show an argument that links back and justifies your stand.
  • Opinions and conclusions should be presented clearly and supported with specific, accurate and relevant evidence (data and statistics) and case studies.
  • Avoid regurgitation and repetition in the essay without processing and adapting content to answer the question and provide good elaboration suited to the question and the essay (this is also applicable to answers for structured questions).
