topics.title: Geographical Concepts
topics.notesHtml:
Strong essay responses are able to:

  • Synthesise three or more concepts in a well-structured way and utilise case studies in body paragraphs to aid explanation of a focused geographical concept (note that as much as concepts are important, evidence is equally important too).
  • Offer a critical evaluation of the statement.
  • Introduce and discuss the issue from different perspectives.
  • Provide new insights and a different perspective that "wows" the examiner.
  • Key idea: discuss how there are multiple perspectives to a certain issue under a broad geographical concept. For example, under the geographical concept of space, the impacts of climate change can be discussed — how does space result in positive and negative impacts in certain regions? E.g. positive impacts: food can now be grown in cooler highlands, with a longer growing season; negative impacts: more extreme weather events resulting in lower crop yield, and some crops can no longer be grown in certain regions.

Concept of Place

Using this concept, we can understand how a more economically developed country (MEDC) is better able to adopt measures and responses compared to a less economically developed country (LEDC). This is because the MEDC has more resources, both financially and in terms of technology and manpower, and is thus more able to implement them compared to an LEDC, which lacks all these. The advancement of communication networks, which is also a limitation due to economic constraints, is also related to the concept of place.

In different countries, especially between MEDCs and LEDCs, the economic and social context varies. For example, if a country's economic and social context is good, the country will have the money to prepare well, and its people will be able to understand preparedness measures (especially emergency drills) since they are literate and educated, compared to a country with a poor economic and social context, where the government cannot fund high-level preparedness measures and the less-educated people would not be able to understand them.

Think of places in terms of geographical, political, and economic places. Places can be compared according to cultural or physical diversity, or disparities in wealth or resource endowment — for example, MEDCs and LEDCs. How do places fit into your argument?

Concept of Power

Power also plays a role, as governments hold the power to decide what measures and responses to take. The result of these measures may differ depending on the government and its actions taken. However, power could also refer to the magnitude of an earthquake, which an emergency drill may not adequately prepare for. Corrupt governments in LEDCs versus more stable governments in MEDCs (Concept of Place).

Power is the ability to influence and affect change or equilibrium at different scales. Power is vested in citizens, governments, institutions and other players, and in physical processes in the natural world (environmental/climatological hazards). Equity and security, both environmental and economic, can be gained or lost as a result of the interaction of powerful forces.

Concept of Possibilities

Discussing how, over time, eventually in a hypothetical situation… Possibilities refer to the opportunities that arise from a certain issue. They are the alternative events, futures and outcomes that geographers can model, project or predict with varying degrees of certainty.

Concept of Processes

Processes are human or physical mechanisms of change (i.e. something ongoing), such as migration or weathering. They operate on varying timescales. Linear systems, circular systems, and complex systems are all outcomes of the way in which processes operate and interact.

Concept of Scale

Scale, at a basic definition, has to do with proportionality. It has both temporal and spatial perspectives. For example, we can look at a short or longer period of time, or the impact of something on either a small area or a global scale. For example, climate change affects the world at a planetary level, thereby requiring all countries to contribute to fighting it (a global/large-scale response).

Concept of Spatial Interaction

Spatial refers to a geographic space, with distribution or location across a landscape or surface. Spatial interaction is the simulation and representation of flows of activity between activities in a geographic space, thereby linking places together. Flows can be physical, such as traffic or migration, or ethereal, like the flow of information and digital technology between countries. These interactions can cause two places to become interdependent and reliant on one another.

Concept of Time

The concept of time often plays a role in varying the effectiveness of measures and responses — for example, during a search and rescue operation, time is a limiting factor, while for warning systems, warnings may not reach people in time to prepare adequately, thus varying the outcome of these measures. The limitation of communications is also linked to time, as the more advanced the communication network, the faster it sends out warnings. (Long term, short term, effect of changing time.)

Concept of People

Often, the mindsets of people play a role as a limiting factor to measures and responses.

To close off this topic, the truth remains that none of the solutions stated previously are perfect, and there is no single solution possible for every country. Thus, only the timeliness and effectiveness of the government, as well as the rest of the concepts mentioned above, can influence the success and effectiveness of the responses.

topics.title: Causes of Climate Change (Natural and Anthropogenic)
topics.notesHtml:
Natural Causes

In 1991, Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted, releasing an estimated 20 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide and ash particles more than 20 km up into the atmosphere. The sulphur-based particles reflected solar energy back into space and lowered temperatures in the northern hemisphere by as much as 0.6°C.

Over the past century, Earth's average temperature has increased by approximately 0.6 degrees Celsius. Solar heating accounts for about 0.15°C, or 25%, of this change, according to computer modelling results published by NASA. Solar variations are expected to continue to modulate both warming and cooling trends at the level of 0.1 to 0.2 degrees Celsius over many years.

Anthropogenic Causes

The world's usage of fossil fuels has increased in recent years. Billions of tonnes of carbon dioxide are released into the atmosphere each year. Carbon emissions from fossil fuels grew 1.5% in 2017, 0.89% in 2018, and were expected to reach 36.81 billion tonnes in 2019.

Globally, trash released nearly 800 million metric tons (882 million tons) of CO2 equivalent in 2010 — about 11 percent of all methane generated by humans. At the landfill, the food and yard waste that trash contains is decomposing and releasing methane, a greenhouse gas that's 28 times more potent than carbon dioxide.

According to the best current estimate, 11 percent of all global greenhouse gas emissions were caused by deforestation, amounting to 284 km² — an area 83 times the size of New York's Central Park — in January 2020 alone, with 10 million km² of forest estimated to have been lost since the beginning of the 20th century.

topics.title: Impacts of Climate Change (Positive and Negative)
topics.notesHtml:
Positive Impacts

In the long term, shipping commerce will benefit from the opening of the Northwest Passage through Canada's formerly icy north for longer periods of the year, due to the loss of Arctic sea ice, as trade is made easier and cheaper. Shorter travel distances of up to 40% between Asia and Europe are possible, with around 5% of the world's trade potentially shipped through the Northern Sea Route (NSR) in the Arctic alone under year-round and unhampered navigability, generating additional income for many European and East Asian countries.

In 2019, there were increases in temperature of 3.4°C to 9.1°C in mid-winter and increases of 1.9°C to 5.7°C in mid-summer in Siberia, making the temperature warmer and more habitable for people.

In the UK, new crops such as blackberries, citrus fruits and maize can now be cultivated. The 1961–1990 average UK growing season was 252 days, but the average for the first years of the 21st century increased to up to 270 days.

Negative Impacts

According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), 33% of coastal land and wetland habitats are likely to be lost in the next hundred years if sea levels continue to rise at current rates. In Cuddalore district in Tamil Nadu, sea level rise turned large tracts of agricultural land in the village into wasteland.

According to the IPCC, the rise in temperatures, along with projected increases in population, could put 5 to 6 billion people at risk of contracting dengue fever in the 2080s.

topics.title: Responses to Climate Change (SG Green Plan, Kyoto Protocol, Paris Agreement)
topics.notesHtml:
Singapore Green Plan

The Singapore Green Plan 2012 aimed to generate 60% of Singapore's energy needs using natural gas by 2021, but as early as 2010, about 79% of Singapore's electricity was already being generated from natural gas — exceeding the Ministry's target ahead of schedule. (However, natural gas requires complex treatment plants to process and pipelines to transport. These pipelines have high maintenance costs because they need to be laid underground and checked regularly for leakage.)

The Building Construction Authority (BCA) Green Mark Scheme aimed to encourage developers and owners to build and maintain greener buildings and achieve a 28% energy efficiency improvement from 2005 building codes. Major retrofitting works, like open-sided building concepts and fitting high-performance glass, help buildings achieve energy savings of between 20% and 40%. The National Library Building and the Park Royal Hotel on Pickering reported energy savings of 15% to 35% compared to conventional buildings. (Limitation: more expensive to build due to expensive material costs, so this is less popular with developers.)

  • New registrations of diesel cars and taxis to cease from 2025.
  • 8 EV-ready towns with chargers at all HDB carparks by 2025.
  • All new car and taxi registrations to be of cleaner-energy models from 2030.
  • 60,000 charging points nationwide, including 40,000 in public carparks and 20,000 in private premises, by 2030.
  • Expand cycling network to 1,320 km by 2030.
  • Increase rail network to 360 km by early 2030s.
  • Increase share of trips taken on mass public transport to 75% by 2030.

(Making public transport more appealing by increasing frequency and access, and by making car ownership more expensive. Limitation: due to the rising standard of living and wealth of Singaporeans, many are still prepared to buy cars.)

Kyoto Protocol

10 years into the Kyoto Protocol, in 2015 the UNFCCC showed that many countries with targets under the Protocol collectively met or exceeded their targets by over 20 percent, due to constant monitoring and reporting by countries for self- and peer-assessment. Between 1990 and 2012, the original Kyoto Protocol parties reduced their CO2 emissions by 12.5%, well beyond the 2012 target of 4.7% (CO2 only, rather than all greenhouse gases, and including Canada).

The Kyoto Protocol was also successful in encouraging sustainable development through the Clean Development Mechanism, whereby developed countries are encouraged to work with developing countries on carbon-reducing projects in exchange for earning carbon credits for helping developing countries develop sustainably.

Limitations:

  • Not enforced — it did not make it compulsory for countries with low greenhouse gas emissions to provide support (such as energy-efficient technology) to countries with high greenhouse gas emissions, so developing countries may not have been able to achieve their emission targets easily.
  • Not all countries were able to meet their goals, and not all countries had the same emission targets.
  • Since 1997, the world's carbon dioxide emissions have increased by 51%. Countries which did not sign the Protocol continued to contribute significantly to global emissions — the United States, India and China (countries that did not sign the Protocol, though some, like China and India, joined after 2011) contribute 42% of the world's carbon dioxide emissions.

Paris Agreement

The Climate Action Tracker (CAT) rates The Gambia's climate targets and policies as "1.5°C Paris Agreement compatible". One of the pillars of The Gambia's strategy to achieve its emission reduction targets is the uptake of renewable energy technologies. After a slow start, The Gambia is now rapidly increasing its renewable energy capacity, with a total of 170 MW in solar PV projects in the pipeline for 2021–2025, with partial finance from the World Bank and the European Investment Bank.

The CAT rates the UK's Paris Agreement climate targets and policies as "Almost sufficient". Considerable progress has been made in decarbonising the UK's power sector, with 43% of electricity generated in 2020 coming from renewable sources, while coal fell to just 1.7% of total generation. In mid-2021, the government confirmed it would bring forward the phase-out of coal from the power sector by one year, from 2025 to 2024. Strong recent increases in offshore wind capacity are set to accelerate, with a recent commitment to reach 40 GW in total installed capacity by 2030. Onshore wind and solar PV were permitted to compete in renewables auctions in 2021, for the first time in six years.

Limitation of rising emissions: global greenhouse gas emissions have continued to grow, with a billion tonnes of CO2 added to annual figures between 2015 and 2018. Advanced economies are not cutting emissions fast or consistently enough to offset growth elsewhere. (The UK is on track for only a 54–56% reduction below 1990 levels by 2030, well below its 2030 target of at least a 68% reduction below 1990 levels.)

topics.title: Mitigation and Adaptation to Climate Change
topics.notesHtml:
Mitigation

The Empire State Building was recently retrofitted with 6,514 windows and reused 96% of old materials. Until 2008, the Empire State Building used energy equivalent to 40,000 single-family homes in a single day. After retrofitting, the building is more energy efficient and its energy use was reduced by 38%. It saved up to 4,000 metric tons of carbon by 2012, equivalent to the offset provided by 750 acres of pine forests.

Promoting public transport use: increased public transport use reduces carbon emissions. US public transport has been found to save 37 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions annually.

Adaptation

Netherlands: a storm surge barrier consisting of 13 dams was built near Rotterdam that can protect the city from storm surges 3m higher than normal. They also built floating homes that remain stable despite the water around them rising and falling. This is an example of how a low-lying country has taken measures to adapt to rising sea levels.

Bangladesh: spent over 10 billion dollars to combat climate change. For example, they have floating vegetable gardens that rise and fall with the water. During the monsoon season, these also double as shelter for cattle and poultry.

topics.title: Coastal Management Measures (Soft and Hard)
topics.notesHtml:
Soft Coastal Protection Measures

Indonesia (East coast of Kalimantan and East coast of Sumatra): according to World Bank data, in an area with 26,705 km² of mangrove area, the area subject to coastal erosion by storm surge was 37,904 km² without mangroves and 27,865 km² with mangroves — a 26.5% decrease.

UK, Lincshore: 530,000 m³ of sand were pumped from licensed offshore sites onto 20 km of beach in 2013, protecting 30,000 properties and 35,000 hectares of land from tidal floods. Watching the new beach being created in front of the promenade has actually become a tourist attraction, and on a sunny day there can often be quite a crowd. Annual cost is about £6 million.

Kapuhenwala and Wanduruppa, two villages in a lagoon in southern Sri Lanka, show the importance of mangroves in saving lives: Kapuhenwala, surrounded by 200 hectares of dense mangroves and scrub forest, saw the 2004 tsunami kill only two people — the lowest number of tsunami-related fatalities in a Sri Lankan village — versus Wanduruppa, surrounded by degraded mangroves, which was severely affected with 5,000 to 6,000 deaths in the district.

Hard Coastal Protection Measures

Ishinomaki City: the 2011 Japan tsunami caused severe damage — areas without breakwaters had 87% of buildings swept away, versus areas with breakwaters, which were protected, with only approximately 25% of buildings damaged.

Mappleton, UK: in 1990, this popular tourist destination was under threat of losing 30 houses. In 1991, hard engineering measures like revetments and two large rock groynes were built (GBP 2 million). Today, farmlands and tourist sites such as caravan parks and villages remain, despite being under threat over 20 years ago.

Pondicherry, India: the city is protected by a seawall which stretches 2 kilometres along its coastline, reaching a height of 27 feet above sea level. When a 24-foot high tsunami caused by the 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake struck Pondicherry, the city centre stayed dry, and casualties were limited to about 600, most of whom were residing in villages outside the protective barrier offered by the seawall.

topics.title: River Management Measures (Soft and Hard)
topics.notesHtml:
Soft River Protection Measures

Pickering, Yorkshire: the Slowing the Flow scheme was enacted in 2009, after the town had suffered four serious floods in 10 years, with the flooding in 2007 estimated to have caused about £7 million of damage. According to The Guardian, the 40,000 trees planted in Yorkshire as part of the scheme (reforestation) successfully reduced peak river flow by 20% during a 2016 flood, when 50mm of rain fell in 36 hours, thereby preventing widespread damage to houses and the town museum.

UK, Dagenham, Beam Washlands: a £4.5 million capital scheme to make space for water and reduce the risk of flooding to 570 homes, 90 businesses (including the Ford Dagenham plant), major infrastructure (including Barking power station), and strategic development sites.

Hard River Protection Measures

Mississippi River: raised embankments and artificial levees. Samuel Muñoz, a geoscientist from Northeastern University, compared results across flood records and found that overall flood risk has gone up 20 percent, with 75% of that risk coming from human engineering of the Mississippi for navigation and flood control. In the 2019 flood season, artificial levee breaches along the Mississippi River cost the US government a total of US$1.9 billion to repair.

Ebro River Basin, Spain: studies showed that reservoirs were very efficient in reducing peak flows in their neighbouring downstream zones, by as much as 80%. Additionally, the global effect of dams and reservoirs on the mouth of the River Ebro reduced overall peak flows by around 57%. (Dams reduce the risk of flooding.)

topics.title: Causes of Globalisation
topics.notesHtml:
Increased movement of people

  • US: in absolute numbers, the United States has a larger immigrant population than any other country, with 47 million immigrants as of 2015. This represents 19.1% of the 244 million international migrants worldwide, and 14.4% of the US population.
  • According to the UN, the estimated number of international migrants worldwide increased between 2000 and 2020, reaching 281 million in 2020 — up from 248 million in 2015, 220 million in 2010, 191 million in 2005 and 173 million in 2000. Increasing migration and tourism make populations more unified and diversified, with more people using, adopting and consuming increasingly similar food, clothes, music and values.

Increased capital mobility and increase in Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) linking global economies

  • Singapore is an extremely globalised nation that has based its economic development on a proactive strategy to attract FDI using its trade openness. According to UNCTAD's World Investment Report 2020, FDI inflows rose to USD 92 billion in 2019, from USD 79 billion a year earlier. Singapore is the 5th largest recipient of FDI inflows in the world, behind the United States, China, the Netherlands and Hong Kong — all heavily globalised countries.
  • In Singapore, at the HS6 digit level, 4,257 products are exported to 220 countries and 4,307 products are imported from 221 countries. The total value of exports (FOB) is US$390,332 million, while the total value of imports (CIF) is US$358,975 million.

Reduced trade barriers and reduced tariffs encouraging trade

  • The North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), signed in 1994, created the world's largest free trade area of 454 million people, effectively linking the economies of the US, Canada and Mexico. According to the US International Trade Commission, between 1993 and 2019, trade between the three members quadrupled from US$290 billion to US$1.23 trillion as a result of NAFTA.
  • Tariff reduction/elimination for 81% of Singapore's exports to India make Singapore-originating products more competitive and allow Singapore exporters to increase their exports to India's large consumer market. Products that benefit include food products, plastics, electronics, pharmaceuticals, and mechanical appliances.

Improvements in transportation

  • From 1993 to 2002, the average shipping distance increased by 40%. Improvements in shipping technology can also lead to innovations such as the Maersk Triple E shipping tanker, which can carry up to 2,500 more containers and has a 16% increase in capacity compared to other ships. The Maersk Triple E also reduces fuel consumption by 37%, reducing the cost of fuel.
  • In 1956, it took up to 1 week to load a single ship. In contrast, with improvements in technology such as mechanised loading, loading times were reduced to 5 hours by 2015.

Improvements in technology

  • The number of internet users around the world increased from 361 million in 2000 to 3 billion in 2015. The internet provides lower barriers of entry, lower cost, and faster and greater return on investment than any other communication channel in human history. In 2017, there were over 8.4 billion devices connected to the internet, forecasted to increase to 13.8 billion in 2021.
  • From 1995 to 2015, there was a 72% increase in the world's internet access, from 13% in 1995 to 85% in 2015. Currently, there are 850 million users of iCloud. The internet is the fastest-growing mode of communication, taking just 4 years to reach 50 million users, compared to radio and television, which took 38 years and 13 years respectively.

topics.title: Impacts of Globalisation
topics.notesHtml:
Increased job opportunities (Socio-economic)

Increased job opportunities and a means for rural poverty reduction: with globalisation and the rise of TNCs, more companies are practising offshoring. This provides those in rural areas with a stable income, as despite a relatively low wage of US$2–3 a day, it is still more than most rural incomes. Since 1990, with increasing globalisation, 1 billion people have been lifted out of poverty, with 600 million lifted between 1992 and 2015 in China alone.

Breakdown of socio-cultural barriers resulting in increased cultural diversity (Social)

Travel around the world is more accessible than ever, facilitating the breakdown of socio-cultural barriers between people and increasing cultural diversity. According to the International Civil Aviation Organisation, the 4.3 billion airline passengers carried in 2018 are expected to grow to about 10 billion by 2040, with the number of departures projected to rise to 90 million in 2040.

Singapore: integration of Malay, Indian, Eurasian, Western and Chinese immigrant food, culture, festivals, dressing, and services catered to them, like Chinatown and Little India.

Increase in power and dominance of global organisations like the UN (Political)

The United Nations (UN) is a global organisation that has significantly contributed to the betterment of the human race. The UN administers the World Food Programme (WFP), an initiative aiming to eradicate hunger and malnutrition globally. The world's largest humanitarian agency, the WFP helps almost 100 million people in approximately 88 countries with assistance every year through food or cash distributions and more.

Increased global cooperation leading to unified efforts to combat climate change (Environmental)

Examples: Paris Agreement, Kyoto Protocol, United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), Montreal Protocol.

Increased exploitation of labour in LEDCs (Socio-economic)

Tens of thousands of female migrant workers from Asia and Africa work in the Middle East as domestic workers, where the Kafala "sponsorship system" continues to drive economic growth whilst leaving workers vulnerable to abuse. The system denies migrant workers their right to freedom of movement — the employer controls the mobility of the worker through control over critical documents such as passports and legal control over their ability to change employment or exit the country.

Threat to local cultures (Social)

Globalisation brings about Westernisation across countries, causing shifts towards Western habits, which come with a more sedentary lifestyle and change in diet. In Nigeria, a country experiencing rapid development as a result of globalisation, over one in five women were reported to be overweight or obese. Women of higher socio-economic status were three and a half times more likely to be overweight or obese compared to those in the lowest status bracket.

Unsustainable increase in global energy demand (Environmental)

From 1990 to 2015, the total warming effect of greenhouse gases released by fossil fuels increased by 37%. Increasing demand for energy (with increasing globalisation) leads to more electricity consumption, with the amount of electricity used per year currently double that of 2000. Since fossil fuels provide 80% of total electricity, there will be increased demand for fossil fuels, resulting in more greenhouse gas emissions, causing increases in global temperatures and accelerating the rate of global warming.

topics.title: Transnational Corporations (TNCs)
topics.notesHtml:
Reinvestment into communities and LEDCs (Socio-economic)

In 2000, the multinational oil and gas company Shell launched and subsequently provided a US$250 million endowment to the Shell Foundation, a charitable organisation aiming to alleviate poverty in Africa and Asia through increasing communities' access to energy and sustainable mobility. According to official figures from the charity's website, the Shell Foundation has to date reduced 48.15 million tonnes of carbon emissions, supported 584,297 jobs, and improved the livelihoods of 193.7 million people. The Foundation also contributed to the UN Investment Climate Facility for Africa with a US$2.5 million investment over 5 years.

Increased employment and wages (Socio-economic)

In the Netherlands, foreign-owned transnational companies created over 700,000 full-time equivalent employment positions in 2014. These organisations also contributed another 650,000 FTEs indirectly to other companies within the nation, with most involved in either trade or manufacturing. 20% of all full-time jobs in the Netherlands are created because of the presence of these organisations.

TNCs such as Daewoo (Republic of Korea) have been attracted to Bangladesh because of low wage rates compared to other Asian countries, and 'spare' quotas to supply ready-made clothes to the European Union and the US. In 1980, Daewoo signed an agreement with a medium-sized Bangladeshi garment firm (Desh Garment Company). Since then, garment exports have increased dramatically, and by 1992 accounted for 46% of Bangladesh's total export earnings. Daewoo provided training programmes, start-up capital and international marketing expertise. Within the Export Processing Zones (EPZs) in Bangladesh, other Korean TNCs have invested heavily in food processing, electrical machinery and chemical industries. (This shows improvement of the country's economy and workforce, and a multiplier effect.)

Siemens, the German engineering and electrical giant, first announced its intention to build a £1.1 billion semiconductor plant in North Tyneside in 1995. After receiving a British government grant of several £million, the factory opened in 1997, creating nearly 800 jobs.

Environmental destruction (Environmental/Social — Forced Displacement)

In December 1984, an explosion at a pesticide plant in Bhopal, India, owned by the American multinational Union Carbide, led to deadly gas fumes leaking into the surrounding atmosphere and toxic chemicals seeping into the ground. In addition to the 3,000 people who died immediately, over the following 25 years there have been a further 20,000 deaths and 120,000 cases of people suffering from health problems, including severe deformities and blindness, as a result of the toxic seepage from the plant into the surrounding area.

Exploitation of workforce in LEDCs (Socio-economic)

An internal investigation conducted by Nike found cases of "abusive treatment", physical and verbal, in more than a quarter of its South Asian plants. Further investigations also revealed that between 25% and 50% of factories in the region restrict access to toilets and drinking water during the workday. In more than half of Nike's factories, employees were forced to work more than 60 hours a week, with those unwilling to do overtime punished severely. In up to 25% of these factories, workers' wages were also far below the legal minimum requirement.

shortAnswer.prompt: Using the Shell Foundation and Netherlands TNC examples, explain the positive socio-economic impacts of TNCs.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: TNCs can bring significant positive socio-economic impacts through reinvestment and job creation. The Shell Foundation, established with a US$250 million endowment in 2000, has reduced 48.15 million tonnes of carbon emissions, supported 584,297 jobs, and improved livelihoods of 193.7 million people, also investing US$2.5 million in the UN Investment Climate Facility for Africa. Similarly, in the Netherlands, foreign-owned TNCs created over 700,000 full-time equivalent jobs directly and 650,000 indirectly in 2014, accounting for 20% of all full-time jobs in the country, mostly in trade and manufacturing.

Cites Netherlands FTE job creation figures and 20% statistic
Links both examples to positive socio-economic impact

shortAnswer.prompt: Discuss the negative impacts of TNCs on host countries, using the Bhopal disaster and Nike labour practices as evidence.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: TNCs can cause severe negative environmental and social impacts in host countries. In December 1984, an explosion at Union Carbide's pesticide plant in Bhopal, India, caused deadly gas leaks and toxic seepage, killing 3,000 people immediately and causing a further 20,000 deaths and 120,000 health cases (including deformities and blindness) over the next 25 years. Additionally, TNCs can exploit labour in LEDCs: Nike's internal investigation found abusive treatment in more than a quarter of its South Asian plants, with 25-50% of factories restricting toilet/water access, and more than half forcing over 60-hour work weeks with severe punishment for refusal, while up to 25% paid below the legal minimum wage.

Cites Nike labour exploitation statistics
